job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Here's a section-by-section read of S. 2817 as pasted. I've flagged the items I think matter most for the story at the end.

**Sec. 2(1)(A) — definition of "commercial deep seabed mining"**

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "by a single vessel."** The 10,000-ton threshold is measured per vessel, so an operator can split production across two or more vessels (or a vessel plus barges, or seabed collectors tethered to different support ships) and never trigger the prohibition. Fleet-splitting is the single most obvious workaround in the bill.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "per year."** The bill doesn't say calendar year, fiscal year, rolling 12 months, or year from first recovery. Under a calendar-year reading, a vessel could recover 10,000 tons in December and another 10,000 in January without ever exceeding the annual cap.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "10,000 metric tons."** No basis for measurement: wet or dry weight, as lifted or as landed, and whether sediment and overburden brought up with nodules count. Polymetallic nodules can be roughly a third water by weight, so the choice of basis changes the real threshold substantially.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "mineral resources" undefined.** On its face, "recovery of … other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel" describes deepwater oil and gas production (drillships, FPSOs), since petroleum is treated as a "mineral" in other federal statutes such as OCSLA. The bill likely intends hard minerals (compare DSHMRA's "hard mineral resource"), but as written it either sweeps in offshore hydrocarbons or invites an argument that it does — a litigation hook either way.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "from the seabed."** Massive sulfide deposits and cobalt crusts are extracted from below the seabed surface or from seamount flanks, and "seabed" vs. "subsoil" is a distinction that matters in the law of the sea. An operator could argue that cutting into the subsoil is not recovery "from the seabed."

6. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "recovery" only.** The definition covers lifting material but not the surrounding activity: collector-vehicle operation, dewatering and plume discharge, transshipment, at-sea or onshore processing, or transport. Most of the environmental concern driving the bill involves activities other than the act of recovery itself.

7. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "vessel."** A fixed or moored platform, or an autonomous seabed system that isn't a "vessel" under the general definition in 1 U.S.C. 3 (a watercraft used as a means of transportation), may fall outside the definition entirely.

8. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — 200-meter depth.** Mining on the continental shelf shallower than 200 meters is not covered, and the bill doesn't say whether depth is measured at the point of extraction or by charted water depth, which matters on slopes and seamounts.

**Sec. 2(1)(B) — Secretary's determination**

9. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — "the Secretary" is never defined.** The bill mentions NOAA (Commerce) and the Secretary of State, but no definition identifies which Secretary makes this determination. That is a straightforward drafting defect that would have to be fixed before the authority could be used.

10. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — no process or standard.** The determination has no rulemaking requirement, no notice, no criteria beyond "comparable" risk, no judicial-review provision, and no statement of whether it applies prospectively only. Because Sec. 5(b) attaches up to 10 years' imprisonment to this definition, a determination-based prosecution would face vagueness and fair-notice challenges.

11. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — comparison to a threshold, not an activity.** Subparagraph (A) describes a tonnage level, not a kind of activity, so "risks comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A)" has no clear referent. It's unclear whether the Secretary is comparing against 10,001-ton nodule mining, against mining generally, or against something else.

**Sec. 2(2) — "U.S. person"**

12. **Sec. 2(2) — foreign subsidiaries.** A corporation organized under a foreign jurisdiction is not a U.S. person even if wholly owned and controlled by a U.S. company. The extraterritorial prong of Sec. 3(a) can be avoided by running the operation through a foreign-incorporated subsidiary — the standard structure in this industry already.

13. **Sec. 2(2) — entity types.** "Corporation" leaves out LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and other entities, and "laws of a State" leaves out entities organized under the laws of the District of Columbia, U.S. territories, or tribal law. Compare the broader "United States person" definitions in sanctions and export-control statutes.

14. **Sec. 2(2) — individuals.** Only citizens are covered; lawful permanent residents and others residing in the U.S. are not, unless they act "in the United States" under Sec. 3(a).

**Sec. 2(3) — "covered vessel"**

15. **Sec. 2(3) — 5,000-gross-ton floor and "equipped."** Smaller vessels never register, and "equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources" is avoidable by staging equipment on a separate support ship or installing it after registration deadlines (there are none — see item 22). The threshold also doesn't align with the 10,000-ton prohibition, so the registry may not capture the vessels that matter.

16. **Sec. 2(3)/Sec. 4 — no jurisdictional nexus.** "Covered vessel" and "operator" have no U.S. connection (flag, ownership, port call), so Sec. 4 purports to require registration by every qualifying vessel in the world. That is unenforceable and invites a challenge on extraterritoriality.

**Sec. 3(a) — prohibition**

17. **Sec. 3(a) — "in the United States."** Mining happens at sea, and the EEZ and outer continental shelf are generally not "in the United States" as that phrase is used in federal statutes. Without an express reference to the territorial sea, EEZ, and OCS, a foreign operator working on the U.S. continental shelf may fall outside the territorial prong.

18. **Sec. 3(a) — U.S.-flagged vessels.** The prohibition reaches persons, not vessels, so a foreign-owned company operating a U.S.-flagged vessel on the high seas isn't clearly covered. Flag-state jurisdiction is the most conventional hook for high-seas conduct, and the bill doesn't use it.

19. **Sec. 3(a) — "engage in" undefined.** The bill doesn't reach financing, chartering, insuring, supplying, crewing, processing, or purchasing output from mining. Combined with item 12, a U.S. company can fund a foreign subsidiary's operation and process the ore in the United States without violating Sec. 3.

20. **Sec. 3(a) — no import restriction.** There is no prohibition on importing or selling minerals recovered by deep seabed mining, so the U.S. market remains fully open to foreign-mined product. Other resource prohibitions (e.g., the Lacey Act, conflict-minerals rules) typically attach to trade as well as extraction.

**Sec. 3(b) — existing operations**

21. **Sec. 3(b) — "exploration license" mismatch.** NOAA under DSHMRA issues exploration *licenses* and separate commercial recovery *permits*, and the International Seabed Authority issues exploration *contracts*. An exploration license doesn't authorize commercial recovery, so this exemption either exempts nothing or — on a broad reading of "conducted under" — exempts any commercial mining by anyone who holds any pre-enactment exploration instrument from any issuer, foreign or domestic.

22. **Sec. 3(b) — no issuer, no end date, no scope limits.** The exemption doesn't say who must have issued the license, whether renewals, extensions, amendments, or transfers after enactment still qualify, whether the operation must already have begun, or whether it is capped at the license's original area and tonnage. As written it is a permanent grandfather clause that could cover operations that haven't started.

23. **Sec. 3(b) — timing.** The cutoff is the date of enactment, so there is an open window between now and signature (and companies that filed DSHMRA applications in 2025 after EO 14285 would have an incentive to get licenses issued before then). Note the bill does not amend DSHMRA, so NOAA retains authority to issue new licenses and commercial recovery permits — see item 33.

**Sec. 3(c) — environmental assessment**

24. **Sec. 3(c) — purpose-based exemption with no limits.** There is no tonnage cap, no permit, no agency approval, no definition of "environmental assessment," and no rule for mixed purposes. A pilot-mining or collector test — which is exactly how the industry already characterizes its pre-commercial operations — can be labeled environmental assessment and recover unlimited material.

25. **Sec. 3(c) — burden of proof.** The bill doesn't say who must prove the purpose or how, which weakens any enforcement action and means the government would litigate operator intent in every case.

**Sec. 4 — registry**

26. **Sec. 4(a) — no deadline, no content, no rulemaking authority.** The bill doesn't say when registration is due, what information is required, or that NOAA may issue regulations, and it gives NOAA no authority to deny, condition, or revoke a registration.

27. **Sec. 4(a)–(b) — no penalty.** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3, so failing to register or to file reports has no statutory consequence. False certifications might be reachable under 18 U.S.C. 1001, but the bill doesn't say so.

28. **Sec. 4(b) — reports don't capture the threshold.** Quarterly reports "describing the recovery activities" aren't required to state tonnage, depth, or location, so they don't give NOAA the data needed to determine whether the 10,000-ton annual threshold was crossed. Nothing authorizes inspection, boarding, or verification, and nothing requires public disclosure.

**Sec. 5 — penalties**

29. **Sec. 5(a) — "each day on which the violation occurs" vs. an annual threshold.** Because the violation is defined by annual tonnage, it's unclear whether the violation "occurs" only on the day the 10,001st ton is lifted, on every day thereafter, or retroactively on every day of mining that year. The daily penalty could therefore be $1 million or hundreds of millions for the same conduct.

30. **Sec. 5(a) — retroactivity conflict with Sec. 8.** Civil penalties apply to "any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment," but the Act doesn't take effect until 180 days after enactment. Conduct in that window can't be a "violation" of a law not yet in effect, and attempting to penalize it raises due-process problems.

31. **Sec. 5 — no enforcement machinery.** No agency is designated to assess civil penalties or bring actions, there is no procedure (administrative vs. judicial), no judicial-review provision, no statute of limitations, no injunctive-relief or forfeiture authority, and no provision on liability of corporate officers. The Attorney General can presumably prosecute under 5(b), but 5(a) has no clear path to court.

32. **Sec. 5(b) — "willfully" plus a discretionary definition.** Criminal liability turns on definitions that include the Secretary's undefined "comparable risk" determination (item 10) and the purpose-based exemptions (item 24), so a willfulness showing will be hard and a vagueness challenge is foreseeable.

**Sec. 6 — international agreement**

33. **Sec. 6 — deadline attaches to "seek," not to conclusion.** The State Department satisfies the section by attempting negotiation within 18 months; there is no reporting requirement, benchmark, or consequence. Separately, the bill nowhere addresses the existing DSHMRA licensing regime (30 U.S.C. 1401 et seq.) or the ISA, so it neither repeals NOAA's authority to issue commercial recovery permits nor explains how an "equivalent" agreement would interact with either.

**Sec. 7 — duration**

34. **Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b) — direct conflict.** Subsection (a) says the prohibition "shall remain in effect until" Congress acts by joint resolution; subsection (b) says the entire Act expires after 10 years. The two are irreconcilable as drafted, and the sunset would also wipe out the registry.

35. **Sec. 7(a) — surplusage and missing report.** A joint resolution is itself a law requiring presidential signature, so (a) adds nothing a later Congress couldn't do anyway, and it cannot bind a future Congress. No one is directed or funded to commission the National Academies report, there is no deadline, and "serious harm" is undefined.

36. **Sec. 7(b) — no savings clause.** The Act is silent on penalties or enforcement actions pending when it expires. The general savings statute (1 U.S.C. 109) may cover this, but without an express clause expect that to be litigated.

**Sec. 8 — effective date**

37. **Sec. 8 — 180-day delay.** Beyond the Sec. 5(a) conflict (item 30), the delay gives operators a window to ramp up, register pre-enactment licenses (item 23), and position vessels. Sec. 4 has no separate effective date or registration deadline, so the registry may not function for months after that.

**Cross-cutting omissions**

38. **No severability clause.** If the Sec. 2(1)(B) definition or the extraterritorial prong of Sec. 3(a) is struck, the rest of the Act is at risk.

39. **No rulemaking authority anywhere.** Neither NOAA, Commerce, nor State is authorized to issue implementing regulations, which leaves every ambiguity above to be resolved in enforcement actions rather than through notice-and-comment.

40. **No definition of "person," "operator," "seabed," "exploration license," or "Secretary."** "Person" will default to the Dictionary Act (1 U.S.C. 1); the others have no fallback.

---

**If you need to prioritize for the story:** the fleet-splitting threshold (1), the foreign-subsidiary gap (12), the unlimited environmental-assessment exemption (24), the exploration-license grandfather (21–22), the undefined "Secretary" (9), the 7(a)/7(b) conflict (34), and the enactment/effective-date conflict (30) are the items most likely to come up at markup or in any later court challenge. The possible sweep-in of offshore oil and gas (4) is the one most likely to draw an amendment from members who otherwise support the bill.

Two caveats: I'm working from the text as pasted, so if the manager's amendment text on the committee site differs (particularly in Sec. 2 and 3), re-check those items. And I've tried to keep this to drafting and enforceability rather than the policy merits, which is consistent with CPR's no-positions approach — sponsors would characterize several of these (the depth and tonnage thresholds, the assessment exemption) as deliberate choices rather than loopholes, and that's worth reflecting in the piece.
